text: Build a register people can trust
After this you can choose fields that answer actual configuration questions.

A configuration register should connect a defined item to an accepted description, requested changes and evidence of work. Design the fields from the questions the team needs to answer, not from the appearance of a report. Item identity, applicable baseline, decision record, unit history, implementation state, verifier and date are common categories. Make allowed states explicit so "approved," "done," and "unknown" do not mean different things to different people.

items: List the decisions the register must support. You should see: Each critical question has a corresponding field. If not: Remove fields nobody can keep current.
Define identifiers, status values and update roles. You should see: Users enter comparable values. If not: Specify what unknown and not applicable mean.
Connect changes to items and individual units. You should see: The relationship can be followed in either direction. If not: Add links rather than repeating conflicting text.
Sample records and resolve discrepancies. You should see: The data supports a plausible report. If not: Correct definitions or update procedures that cause errors.
An example unit record might show serial 0057, controller release 2.3, accepted drawing R4 and replacement-module work awaiting verification.

text: Define every field before designing a dashboard.
A perfectly formatted table can still contain guesses or stale data.

items: Keeping "current status" as one free-text field It mixes review, approval and physical work. Fix: Use separate, defined state fields.
